newsitem.title: UK: Refuge shareholder to vote against merger.
newsitem.headline: Refuge shareholder to vote against merger.

text.p: At least one major institutional shareholder in UK life assurer Refuge Group has decided to vote against the firm's proposed merger with United Friendly
Perpetual senior investment manager, Neil Woodford, who had already expressed concerns about the terms of the deal, said on Thursday that Perpetual would vote against the merger.

Woodford said this decision was taken on Wednesday after a meeting a week ago with executives of the two companies failed to convince him that Refuge directors had secured the best possible terms for shareholders.
"We are going to be voting against," he told Reuters.
Perpetual owns just over seven percent of Refuge's shares and is one of several institutional shareholders to have voiced concerns about the 1.4 billion stg merger announced this month.

Industry sources said Perpetual may yet change its mind and suggested the tougher stance taken by Woodford may be a negotiating tool to extract better terms or more information for Refuge shareholders. But Woodford said his decision was final.
"There is a lack of information about the merits of the deal," he said. "They are not minded to provide any more."
they had not yet decided how to vote or were not available to comment. An extraordinary meeting to approve the merger has been scheduled for September 9.

"We haven't yet been able to fully study and fully come to a conclusion on all the factors required to make a decision," said Philip May, head of the pension funds team at Prudential Portfolio Managers.
"We obviously like to study the documents and talk to the parties involved," he said.
It is not so much the logic of the deal, but the valuation of Refuge's assets which has upset some of the shareholders.

In particular, they believe that during discussions with the UK government Refuge could have unlocked more "orphan" assets for shareholders from its ordinary branch of business, not just the 430 million stg it identified in the industrial branch.
The orphan assets are those a company holds, which are surplus to meeting policyholder requirements.
"There's 940 million stg sitting there and some of it is ours," said one fund manager. "We want them to change the terms or the structure of the deal."
Senior executives at Refuge and United Friendly could not be reached for comment on Thursday. They were believed to be in Scotland meeting shareholders.
A source close to the companies expressed disappointment at Perpetual's stance, but was confident the merger would proceed.
"It is not going to change our confidence that this deal will go through," he said. "The commercial logic is compelling."
The source stressed that Refuge had been in discussions with the DTI about its inherited estate for 18 months and was happy to talk to shareholders about what was in the public domain.

Other major shareholders in Refuge include Britannic Assurance, Mercury Asset Management (MAM) and Legal & General. Prudential is itself in discussions with the DTI about the possible distribution of orphan estate.
